sections.summary: Paul recounts his visit to Jerusalem fourteen years later, brought by revelation, where he presented his gospel to the recognized leaders privately to ensure his work would not be in vain.

sections.section_title: The Titus Test Case -- Circumcision Refused
sections.summary: Paul reports that Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised in Jerusalem, and that Paul refused to yield to false brothers who infiltrated the community to spy out the freedom believers have in Christ, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved.

The recognized leaders in Jerusalem -- James, Cephas, and John -- added nothing to Paul's gospel but recognized his divine commission and extended the right hand of fellowship, agreeing to a division of labor between the circumcised and uncircumcised missions.

Paul publicly opposed Cephas at Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile table fellowship under pressure from the circumcision party, exposing the hypocrisy of a Jew who lived like a Gentile but then compelled Gentiles to live like Jews.

sections.section_title: Justification by Faith, Not Works of Law
sections.summary: Paul articulates the principle that even Jews by birth recognized that a person is not justified by works of the law but through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, and that by works of the law no one will be justified.

sections.section_title: The Absurdity of Rebuilding What Was Torn Down
sections.summary: Paul argues that if seeking justification in Christ made them sinners then Christ would be a servant of sin, which is absurd, and that rebuilding the law-based system after demolishing it would prove oneself a transgressor.

sections.section_title: Death to the Law, Life to God
sections.summary: Paul declares that through the law he died to the law to live to God, that he has been crucified with Christ, and that his present life is animated by Christ living in him and sustained by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him.
Paul states that he does not nullify the grace of God, because if righteousness could come through the law then Christ died for no purpose.
sections.relevance: The verb atheteo ('to nullify, to set aside, to annul') applied to grace implies that grace can be formally cancelled or rendered void. Paul says he does not nullify grace, but the argument's structure presupposes that someone could -- specifically, by pursuing righteousness through the law. The implication is that grace is not unconditionally operative; a believer's volitional reorientation toward law-based righteousness can set aside the grace of God and render Christ's death pointless for that person. This anticipates the explicit statement of 5:4.
key_phrases: I do not nullify the grace of God
if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose
